vibe.rationale: Vibe 3 — lower edge, directional pressure toward 2, stabilized by Sunday signing window and Senate legislative completion. The June 6 cycle is held at 3 by the continued openness of the private diplomatic channel (Iran comms resolved Day 3, no re-suspension), the reference by Trump and mediators to a Sunday June 7 signing date, and the Senate's clean legislative passage of the DHS/ICE reconciliation package. Against these, the downward pressure is more acute than any prior day in the amendment counter-demand period: Ghalibaf's public 'missiles not talks' statement inverts Trump's relief-for-performance framework at the level of explicit sequencing doctrine, not tactical positioning; the Iran International 8-of-10-conditions breach characterization, if accurate, means the amendment counter-demand has widened the Khamenei-approval gap rather than resolved it; and Hezbollah's rejection of the broader Lebanon framework (Day 3 post-rejection) stresses the durability of the Beirut-suburbs partial truce even as it holds four consecutive days. The bifurcation between private (comms open, Sunday window live) and public (Ghalibaf missiles, 8-of-10 breach) tracks can coexist in a final-compression negotiating dynamic — Iranian diplomatic practice in high-stakes endgame sequences frequently involves public hardening as private deal closure approaches. But if Sunday passes without a signing or a new confirmed timeline, the 'delay not collapse' framing becomes harder to maintain and Vibe 2 becomes the operative assessment. NIFC YTD above 10-year averages; east Cascades explicitly above normal in June; Washington drought emergency Day 2; measles dispersal beginning — structural stresses advance unchanged. Upgrade to 4 requires: Iran accepts amendment counter-demand or Sunday June 7 signing materializes; Beirut-suburbs truce holds Day 5 with no Dahiyeh incident. items.headline: MOU Amendment Counter-Demand Day 2: Ghalibaf 'Concessions Via Missiles'; Draft MOU Breaches 8 of 10 Khamenei Conditions (Iran International); Sunday June 7 Signing Window Referenced by Trump and Mediators; Iran Comms Resolved Day 3; Hormuz Day 99 — D-100 Tomorrow; WPA Day 98 Day 8 Past Hard Deadline
items.summary: The central geopolitical thread on June 6 evening is the Iran deal's widening bifurcation between private diplomatic track and public Iranian posture. The private channel remains confirmed open — Iran comms resolved Day 3 with no re-suspension signal in the June 6 cycle — and both Trump and deal mediators have referenced Sunday June 7 as a potential signing date, the first concrete forward anchor since the June 4–11 ABC News window. But the public Iranian posture has hardened to its most acute point in the amendment counter-demand period. Iranian parliament speaker and lead negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf issued the defining public statement of the June 6 cycle: 'We take concessions not through talks, but with missiles,' and 'No action [opening Hormuz, accepting nuclear limitations] will be taken before the other side acts [lifting the blockade and easing sanctions].' Ghalibaf's statement is a public assertion of Iran-first sequencing that directly inverts Trump's 'relief for performance' framework and the amendment counter-demand's immediate-Hormuz-transfer requirement. Separately and critically, Iran International reported that a state TV pundit who accompanied Iran's negotiating team characterized the draft MOU as breaching 8 of the 10 conditions Mojtaba Khamenei approved — the most specific internal critique of the MOU text to date. If accurate, the amendment counter-demand has widened rather than resolved the Khamenei-approval gap: Mojtaba has endorsed the broad deal template but has not approved the specific MOU text, and the 8-of-10-breach characterization implies the amended text is further from Khamenei approval than the pre-amendment expert-level draft. The deal architecture Trump is seeking: Iran opens Hormuz immediately at signing, mines removed within 30 days, specific enrichment moratorium timelines and HEU removal schedule, 60-day framework period, US sanctions waivers contingent on Hormuz opening, proportional naval blockade lift as commercial shipping resumes. Ghalibaf's sequencing demand (US acts first → Iran acts second) is structurally opposite. These two signals — Ghalibaf public hardening and 8-of-10 breach — can coexist with a Sunday signing in a final-compression dynamic where public rhetoric peaks as private deal closure approaches; or they represent a genuine widening of the deal gap that makes Sunday structurally impossible. The resolution of this ambiguity is the top-priority watch item for June 7. Hormuz closes Day 99; D-100 milestone arrives June 7. CENTCOM self-defense authority remains operative; no kinetic resumption signal in the June 6 cycle. WPA advances to Day 98 (Day 8 past the hard 90-day constitutional deadline) without enforcement, litigation, or congressional emergency action.

items.summary: Six secondary geopolitical threads on June 6 evening. First: Beirut-suburbs partial truce advances to Day 4. The narrow arrangement — Israel not striking Dahiyeh, Hezbollah not attacking Israel — has held through four consecutive days, the longest operative hold in the Lebanon track. Hezbollah's rejection of the broader Lebanon ceasefire framework (Day 3 post-rejection) structurally limits durability: Hezbollah has demanded a comprehensive ceasefire beginning with full Israeli withdrawal from southern Lebanon and has rejected the pilot-zone arrangement brokered June 3. Lebanon ceasefire Day 21 holds; full framework — Israeli withdrawal, Hezbollah disarmament, five-year monitoring regime — remains outstanding; Israel continues south Lebanon strikes. The Iran-Lebanon linkage risk is elevated: Ghalibaf's hardline public statement and the 8-of-10-conditions breach report create a negotiating environment in which Lebanon is a potential Iranian leverage point. Any Israeli action beyond south Lebanon (Dahiyeh strikes, Bekaa Valley resumption) remains the primary mechanical trigger for Iranian comms disruption. Second: House WPA vote (215-208, June 3) advances to Day 3 post-vote. As a concurrent resolution it does not require Trump's signature and cannot be vetoed; it proceeds to the Senate. The Senate previously passed a similar bill in May. The White House stated the resolution 'will not reach' Trump's desk. Trump characterized the vote as 'meaningless' and noted it occurred during 'final negotiations.' Four Republican votes (Fitzpatrick on record); bipartisan signal, not a policy enforcement mechanism. Third: Peru presidential runoff is tomorrow June 7 — Fujimori vs. Sánchez; Fujimori held polling advantage entering the runoff; results shape Andean lithium and copper supply chain politics and US critical minerals diplomacy. Fourth: FIFA World Cup opens globally T-5 (June 11); Seattle's first Lumen Field match T-9 (June 15, Belgium vs Egypt). 'Let's Play SEA '26' 39-day fan celebration at Seattle Center begins June 11. Fifth: CISA extends clean streak to Day 35. No confirmed OT/ICS incident, no FBI IC3 flash. Shamkhani IRGC cyber risk Day 12; no Mojtaba override of Shamkhani's nuclear-rejection statement. Sixth: Acting DNI vacancy Day 16; IC simultaneously managing Iran amendment response window, Lebanon stability assessment, Peru election security, FIFA hacktivist window opening, and hurricane/wildfire season without a Senate-confirmed director.

items.summary: The economic thread on June 6 evening advances the Warsh silence streak to Day 23 with 10 days to the June 16–17 FOMC. CME FedWatch assigns approximately 3% probability to a June rate hike; market consensus is for a hold at 3.50–3.75%. But the structural pressure environment argues against complacency: the Philadelphia Fed Q2 2026 Survey of Professional Forecasters (6.0% annualized CPI — 3.3pp above the prior survey) remains the dominant inflation signal, with no revision or counterweight in the June 6 cycle. Cleveland PCE nowcast holds at 4.18%. Late-2026 hike probability is approximately 70% per multiple analyst readings — the question is not if but when the Warsh Fed tightens. Yardeni Research argued the Fed will have to raise rates in July to appease bond vigilantes. Paul Tudor Jones stated there is 'no chance' Warsh can cut rates. The 30-year Treasury yield at its 5.18% recent high and the 10-year at approximately 4.55% price inflation persistence at a duration presupposing multi-quarter entrenchment. Warsh's Day 23 silence — the longest communicative void of any Fed Chair at this stage of an FOMC cycle in recent history — means the June 16–17 meeting itself (language, dissents, forward guidance tone) carries outsized signaling weight. Any dissent structure implying imminent hike, or any Warsh statement before June 16 that breaks the silence, is the highest-priority economic watch item. Iran deal dynamics transmit directly: if the Sunday June 7 signing window materializes, Brent relief to $85–90 is the immediate economic relief signal; if Sunday fails without a new timeline, Brent upside toward $100+ is the operative risk, accelerating the Q2 SPF inflation read.

items.headline: Senate Passes DHS/ICE Reconciliation 52-47 Early June 6 — Anti-Weaponization Fund Preserved; Cassidy Amendment Blocked (6 GOP Votes); Murkowski Opposed; House Next Week; Markets Navigating Iran Amendment Uncertainty
items.summary: Senate final passage of the DHS/ICE immigration enforcement reconciliation package 52-47 in the early morning of June 6 is the domestic legislative milestone of the cycle. After blocking multiple amendments to strip or limit the $1.776 billion anti-weaponization fund — a settlement fund for Trump-aligned IRS plaintiffs — the Senate completed final passage. Senator Bill Cassidy's amendment to block the fund drew 6 GOP votes but failed; Senator Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) opposed the final package. The package now moves to the House, where Speaker Johnson has indicated a House vote is planned for next week. The 52-47 final passage is distinct from — though overlapping in political dynamics with — the House Reconciliation 2.0 (Big Beautiful) deadlock: the House Freedom Caucus anti-weaponization fund opposition is a separate political track. US equity markets are navigating the Iran amendment uncertainty: the deal confirmation trade (Brent to $85–90, consumer-relief equity uplift) remains contingent on Sunday signing materializing. The S&P and Nasdaq near-record consolidation continues. Ghalibaf's 'missiles not talks' statement and 8-of-10-conditions breach report are being priced as deal-delay signals; market distinction between delay and collapse is the key uncertainty heading into Sunday. AI data center capex (224 GW incremental load through 2035) continues providing a structural equipment-and-construction tailwind while creating wholesale electricity pricing pressure. Labor market cooling continues: below-trend job gains, real wage growth negative in energy-exposed sectors.

items.headline: T-HUD Full Committee Markup Completed June 3 — $92.224B -10.4% From FY26 — Infrastructure Fiscal Inflection Confirmed; Sound Transit $34.5B Gap; Grid Modernization Lagging AI Demand; ASCE BIL Rolloff Risk Advancing
items.summary: T-HUD's June 3 full committee markup completion is the infrastructure fiscal inflection point confirmed in the June 6 cycle. The House Appropriations Committee approved the FY27 T-HUD bill at $92.224 billion — $10.659 billion (10.4%) below FY26 enacted levels. HUD programs specifically: $71.38 billion, down $5.94 billion (approximately 8%) from the $77.3 billion FY26 level. The markup's committee passage makes the -10.4% cut the operative planning baseline for PNW transit operators (Sound Transit, TriMet), Amtrak, and CDBG housing assistance recipients pending floor action and Senate conference. Sound Transit's $34.5 billion funding gap remains unresolved as the Sound Transit board approaches its June capital planning session. Seattle Mayor Wilson's Seattle Transit Measure (doubling city transit sales tax) remains in council consideration — a local offset that cannot close the full federal-match gap. ASCE's 2026 infrastructure progress report identifies the T-HUD -10.4% markup, if enacted, as initiating the infrastructure-progress reversal that post-2026 BIL rolloff projects for FY27 onward: the combination of declining federal appropriations and BIL rolloff creates a structural deficit in transit capital investment. Grid modernization remains acutely behind AI-driven demand growth: 224 GW incremental load forecast through 2035 is outpacing transmission modernization and interconnection queue management, with FERC's summer assessment confirming PNW drought-reduced hydropower as a specific summer vulnerability. SPP, PJM, CAISO retain sufficient summer capacity for expected demand but identify wildfire-drought-heat as tail-risk scenarios.

items.summary: Four secondary domestic threads on June 6 evening. First and most structurally urgent: measles. School dispersal begins June 7 — the transmission network enters its summer mobile phase; school-based contact tracing loses its cluster-resolution utility as students and families diffuse geographically. Geographic distribution: SC 668 (highest), UT 425, TX 180, FL 134; active outbreaks in FL, PA, UT, VA (Central Virginia remains active). 30 outbreaks YTD; 6% of 2,030 cases (approximately 122 patients) hospitalized; more than 92% unvaccinated. PAHO elimination status review (November 2026) is under acute pressure — elimination status loss has downstream implications for public health funding frameworks and global health diplomacy. Second: SCOTUS Alabama redistricting ruling (lower court reversed, expanded state redistricting latitude) is operative in multiple states' 2026 electoral map calculations. Third: California Governor primary remains active — Becerra, Porter, Steyer (Democratic); Bianco, Hilton (Republican). Fourth: Iowa Feenstra Day 2 post-result — agricultural insurgency signal entering broad 2026 midterm analysis.

analyst_summary: June 6, 2026 evening closes at Vibe 3 — lower edge, directional pressure toward 2, stabilized by Sunday June 7 signing window and Senate legislative completion. The cycle's defining tension is the bifurcation between the Iran deal's private track (comms open Day 3, Sunday signing window referenced by Trump and mediators) and public Iranian posture (Ghalibaf 'missiles not talks'; draft MOU reportedly breaches 8 of 10 Khamenei conditions — sharpest internal critique of the text to date). These two signals can coexist in a final-compression negotiating dynamic where public rhetoric peaks as private closure approaches; or they represent a genuine widening of the deal gap that makes Sunday structurally impossible. The critical variable is whether Iran delivers a formal amendment-counter-demand response before Sunday June 7 and what it contains. Hormuz D-100 milestone lands tomorrow. Senate's early-morning 52-47 final passage of the DHS/ICE reconciliation package — anti-weaponization fund preserved over Cassidy amendment challenge — is the domestic legislative milestone of the cycle; House takes it up next week. T-HUD full committee markup at $92.224B (-10.4% from FY26) is the infrastructure fiscal inflection point confirmed: transit capital investment, CDBG, and Amtrak face a structural cut if enacted, with direct Sound Transit federal-match implications. Measles at 2,030 cases begins its summer dispersal arc June 7 — the transmission network enters its summer mobile phase with CDC summer travel warning active. NIFC above-normal Day 6 with east Cascades explicitly above normal in June; YTD national fire pace above 10-year averages on both fires and acres. Washington drought emergency Day 2. FIFA World Cup opens globally in 5 days; Seattle first Lumen Field match in 9; NIFC-FIFA co-response risk window formally open. Tomorrow's watchlist: Iran formal response to amendment counter-demand — Sunday signing is the single highest-priority event; Brent crude Sunday opening; Peru runoff results; Hormuz D-100; Lebanon partial truce Day 5.
